extracted.intended_audience: journalism students and news reporters learning event and feature reporting
extracted.subtask_description: Reporting and writing news items about exhibitions, pageants, openings and public ceremonies — emphasizing how to incorporate speeches, atmosphere, facts, and human-interest incidents into event stories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of speeches and toasts
rubrics_metrics.description: When speeches and toasts are delivered in connection with these events, they are treated like other speeches and are fitted into the story as incidents of the occasion, or, if they are of sufficient significance, they may be played up as the feature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fit speeches into the narrative as incidents unless the speech itself is the newsworthy element; if a speech has sufficient significance, make it the feature of the story. (Verbatim guidance appears near the top of the page.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Include precise factual specifics
rubrics_metrics.description: Give concrete facts: dates, times, locations, committee and officer names, numbers (exhibits, floor space, prices), and organizational details.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples in the text list organizers and managers (e.g., 'Col. George Pope, H. O. Smith, Wilfred C. Leland, and S. A. Miles, manager'), exact opening times ('doors will be unlocked at 2 P. M.'), quantities ('150,000 square feet', '338 exhibits'), and price ranges ('$265 to $7,500') — use similar specifics to establish factual credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Atmospheric scene-setting with sensory detail
rubrics_metrics.description: Use vivid sensory description (sights, sounds, colors, smells) and metaphors to convey the atmosphere of the occasion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The examples employ phrases like 'perfect jumble of color and sound', 'talking moving picture run wild', descriptions of decoration color schemes ('white, gold, and crimson'), and onomatopoeic reporting of animal sounds to create atmosphere. Use such concrete sensory details and apt metaphors to make the scene tangible for readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use human-interest anecdotes and small incidents
rubrics_metrics.description: Include short, telling anecdotes or incidents (comic or poignant) that illustrate the character of the event.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The poultry-show account uses anecdotes (a rooster hitched to a miniature mill that refused to move; trained hens performing on a turnstile) to enliven the report. Such episodes give readers memorable entry points into broader coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incorporate authoritative quotes and statements
rubrics_metrics.description: Include statements, speeches, or letters from officials and organizers to explain the event's significance and broader implications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Mayor Mitchel's remarks about market policy and President Roosevelt's letter praising the tunnel; these quotations supply context, authority, and significance beyond descriptive reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: List participants, organizers and judges to establish scope
rubrics_metrics.description: Name sponsoring organizations, committees, judges, and participating groups to show the event's organization and breadth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text lists numerous societies and committees, judges' names for parade awards, and the composition of exhibition committees — include comparable lists to demonstrate legitimacy and scale of the event (but avoid overwhelming readers with unnecessary names).

rubrics_metrics.name: Note schedules, special days, and practical details
rubrics_metrics.description: Report scheduled special days, admission arrangements, opening hours, and any unique visitor information (e.g., Society Day, Theatrical Day, admission charges, Sunday closures).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The automobile show and market accounts specify special days and hours and note exceptions (e.g., 'first day ... doors will open at 2 P. M., and on other days at 10 A.M., ... Sunday ... closed'). Include such operational details to be useful to readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adapt tone and style to the subject
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose a tone appropriate to the event — from playful and comic to solemn and ceremonial — and adjust wording and emphasis accordingly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare the two automobile-parade accounts (noted on the page) for differences in style and tone: one is straightforward and celebratory, another leans on ironic, smoky-comic images. The textbook explicitly instructs readers to compare these stories 'with reference to style and tone.' Use tone to match the audience and subject matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use vivid leads and concrete details rather than abstractions
rubrics_metrics.description: Open with an engaging, concrete scene or fact (a striking image, number, or action) rather than abstract generalities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many examples begin with concrete images or actions (e.g., 'More than three thousand automobiles... helped to impress upon throngs of spectators', 'The twentieth annual exhibition ... was opened several hours before daybreak with appropriate barnyard pomp and ceremony'). Leads that anchor the reader in a moment increase engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Employ comparative or historical context when relevant
rubrics_metrics.description: Place the event in a comparative or historical framework to clarify its importance or novelty (comparisons with prior years, other places, or historical figures/events).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page references past customs ('Following the custom of former years'), attendance comparisons, and historical notes (e.g., Presidents visiting markets, anniversaries). Such context can amplify significance and help readers understand why the event matters.
